plain_text:
Research shows that Aedes aegypti mosquitoes are
drawn to the smell of humans over other animals, but
it's not clear how they tell the difference. A recent NIH-
funded study suggests that a clue may lie in the ways that
mosquitoes' brains react to different kinds of smells.

plain_text:
Mosquitoes have taste receptors on their feet as well as
their tongue, so once it lands, the mosquito can taste the
host even before it bites. Mosquitoes also have multiple
smell (or “olfactory”) receptors in different locations:
the antennae, the maxillary palp (near the mouth), and
the proboscis (a mouth-like tube that helps the insect
drink). These receptors connect to specific parts of the
mosquito brain called “glomeruli,” which respond to
different kinds of smells.
